Normal: Free up space soon. The Disk Usage Analyzer (baobab), or 'sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h' in a terminal, shows what is using it.
Common space users on Linux: the package cache ('sudo apt clean' or 'sudo dnf clean all'), old system logs ('sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M'), the Trash, and old Snap or Flatpak versions.
Bad: Under 10% free: package updates can fail half-way, and SSDs slow down and wear faster. Free space now, starting with the package cache and the Trash.
If this is /boot, old kernels are the usual cause: 'sudo apt autoremove' (or your distribution's equivalent) removes the ones no longer used.
Consider moving large media folders to another drive or an external disk.

rules.forecast: An SSD kept nearly full has less room for wear leveling — sustained <10% free measurably accelerates wear.

Normal: Memory was fairly full while scanning. If the PC often feels slow, closing browser tabs or adding RAM would help.
Bad: Memory was nearly exhausted, which forces Linux to swap and to drop its file cache, and makes everything feel slow.
Close what you are not using and re-check; the System Monitor, or 'top' sorted by memory (press M), shows what holds the most. If it is always this full, more RAM is the real fix.

Normal: This system uses strict overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory = 2) and has promised most of what it can hand out. 'ps -eo comm,vsz --sort=-vsz | head' lists the programs reserving the most.
Bad: This system uses strict overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory = 2) and is close to its limit: at 100% programs are refused memory and can crash, even with RAM free.
Close what you are not using. More swap raises the limit at once (the limit is swap plus vm.overcommit_ratio percent of RAM); more RAM is the lasting fix.

rules.forecast: When the limit is reached, programs that ask for more memory are refused and may close without saving.

Normal: Linux ran out of memory once since the last restart and closed a program to recover. Worth noting what was open; if it happens again, see the tips for repeated kills.
Bad: Linux ran out of memory more than once since the last restart, and closed a program each time to recover.
'sudo journalctl -k | grep -i "killed process"' names the program each time.

Common causes: a virtual machine or local AI model sized for more RAM than this PC has, many browser tabs, or a program that keeps growing. More swap (or zram) is a quick fix; more RAM is the lasting one.

rules.forecast: Each out-of-memory kill closes a program at once, without a chance to save.

Normal: Warm near the processor. Normal under heavy load; if it stays this high while the PC is doing little, dust or old thermal paste is the usual cause.

This is the firmware's (ACPI) sensor, not the processor's own. The processor's sensor driver (coretemp for Intel, k10temp for AMD) was not found; most distributions load it automatically, so a missing one is worth a look.
Bad: Very hot near the processor. At this level the processor slows itself down to protect itself, so the PC feels slower than it should.
Clean the fan and heatsink. On a laptop several years old, fresh thermal paste often lowers temperatures a lot.
Check the charger is the wattage the laptop needs: an underpowered charger can also hold the processor back.

rules.forecast: Sustained heat shortens the life of every component near it, and thermal shutdowns risk file-system damage.
